strengths: Highly intuitive and well-grounded motivation: Decoupling local realism (using a mode-seeking reverse-KL objective) from global coherence (using a mean-seeking supervised flow-matching objective) directly addresses the major 'blurriness vs. drift' trade-off in long video generation.

The decoupled architecture (utilizing a Decoupled Diffusion Transformer with separate heads sharing a unified encoder) successfully resolves gradient interference between the average-seeking L2 flow matching and the mode-seeking DMD distillation objectives.

Solid technical and engineering contributions, specifically the sliding-window DMD implementation strategy that elegantly resolves the hybrid image-video latent boundary mismatch during windowed crops.
Strong empirical performance across both quantitative VBench/VLM metrics and qualitative comparisons, demonstrating fast, few-step generation that is both sharp and temporally consistent.
weaknesses: The training pipeline (which involves on-policy rollouts, querying the teacher model, and training/updating a fake score estimator) is computationally complex. A detailed analysis of the training wall-clock time and VRAM overhead compared to standard SFT would clarify its accessibility.

The quantitative experiments are primarily conducted on the Wan 1.3B model. Although qualitative results for the 14B model are referenced, presenting quantitative metrics on the larger model would strengthen the evaluation.

strengths: An elegant and conceptually sound motivation: decoupling local realism (using mode-seeking reverse-KL on sliding windows) from global narrative structure (using mean-seeking SFT on full-length videos) effectively addresses the scarce data bottleneck in long-video training.

The proposed Decoupled Diffusion Transformer (DDT) architecture with shared encoder and dual decoder heads cleverly resolves the gradient interference between the mean-seeking and mode-seeking objectives.

Enables fast, high-quality, few-step inference (4 NFEs) by utilizing only the trained Distribution Matching (DM) head at inference time, offering a significant speedup compared to standard multi-step flow matching/diffusion baselines.
Comprehensive evaluation on diverse benchmarks (VBench-Long and Gemini-3-Pro) demonstrates a superior trade-off between local sharpness/motion and long-range consistency.

Practical implementation details, such as handling the image-video latent boundary mismatch during sliding window DMD (detailed in Appendix C), enhance the reproducibility of the method on modern joint image-video latent spaces.
weaknesses: The conceptual components (DDT, DMD/VSD, and Flow Matching) are largely drawn from existing literature (Wang et al. 2025c, Yin et al. 2024b), which slightly limits the algorithmic novelty of the individual blocks.

The performance is inherently bounded by the quality of the frozen short-video teacher; any localized temporal artifact or spatial distortion present in the teacher will inevitably be distilled into the student model.

While the explanation for why some baseline consistency metrics are higher (e.g., due to static content or over-saturation) is convincing, a more formal human preference evaluation or user study would help solidify these claims.

strengths: The paper proposes an elegant decoupling of global coherence (via mean-seeking Flow Matching on long videos) from local realism (via mode-seeking Distribution Matching on sliding windows), directly tackling the scarcity of high-quality long video data.

The architectural choice of using a Decoupled Diffusion Transformer (DDT) with a shared encoder and dual heads (FM and DM) is well-justified, successfully avoiding gradient interference between the conflicting mean-seeking and mode-seeking targets.

The proposed paradigm enables highly efficient, few-step (e.g., 4-step) inference for minute-scale videos, greatly reducing the computational cost of long-video generation compared to standard long-context models.
The authors address key practical challenges in the supplementary material, such as resolving the semantic boundary mismatch between image and video frame latents during sliding-window DMD training.
The qualitative results demonstrate strong visual fidelity and long-term consistency, showing crisp details where standard SFT baselines suffer from blurriness.
weaknesses: In Table 1, the autoregressive baselines (CausVid, Self-Forcing, InfinityRoPE) are evaluated at NFE = 4. Since these methods are generally not designed for few-step generation and require larger NFEs to produce high-quality frames, this comparison may be unfair. It would be much more informative to compare the proposed 4-step model against these baselines at their standard, optimal NFEs (e.g., 20-50 steps).

The paper lacks details on training complexity, VRAM consumption, and optimization stability. Given that on-policy DMD with a dynamically trained 'fake' score estimator can be unstable and costly, a detailed discussion on the training overhead would strengthen the work.

There is no human evaluation or user preference study, which remains a crucial benchmark in generative video tasks because automated metrics (such as VBench and Gemini evaluations) may not always align perfectly with human perception of motion and temporal consistency.

strengths: An elegant and well-motivated concept that decouples global narrative structure (mean-seeking flow matching) from local fidelity (mode-seeking distribution matching) to solve the 'fidelity-horizon' gap in long video generation.

The proposed decoupled architecture utilizing a shared long-context encoder with two distinct heads (FM and DM) effectively mitigates gradient interference between mean-seeking and mode-seeking objectives.
By discarding the FM head and using only the DM head at inference time, the model achieves fast, high-quality, few-step (4 NFE) long-video generation.
Comprehensive and robust evaluation, including VBench-Long metrics, LLM-based consistency metrics, a detailed user study, and systematic ablation studies that validate each component.
weaknesses: High training complexity and overhead. Training requires on-policy student rollouts, evaluation of a frozen teacher, and optimizing a fake score estimator. A quantitative discussion on the training compute overhead and training time compared to standard SFT is missing.

Heavy reliance on existing components. The core blocks (DDT, DMD/VSD, and the latent re-encoding trick from LongLive) are compiled from previous works, making the methodological novelty somewhat incremental, although their synergistic combination is highly effective.

The analysis of the latent prefix re-encoding trick is relatively brief. Given its importance in making sliding-window DMD work on modern latent spaces, a deeper discussion or ablation on this boundary alignment would be beneficial.

strengths: The paper introduces an elegant and conceptually sound framework that decouples global coherence (narrative structure) from local visual fidelity, addressing the fundamental 'fidelity-horizon' trade-off in long video generation.

The proposed Decoupled Diffusion Transformer (DDT) architecture effectively avoids gradient interference by dividing the training signal into a mean-seeking Flow Matching head and a mode-seeking Distribution Matching head, sharing a unified long-context encoder.

The inclusion of a practical solution for the semantic boundary mismatch in sliding-window latent distillation (re-encoding the last frame of the preceding chunk) is highly useful and shows strong engineering attention to detail.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations, including a 1-minute stress test, multi-modal LLM-based evaluation, and a 31-participant user study, consistently demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach over state-of-the-art baselines.
weaknesses: The method still requires access to a high-quality (though scarce) long-video dataset for the global SFT phase, meaning it is not completely independent of long-video data curation challenges.
The proposed latent re-encoding trick (decoding the prefix and re-encoding the last frame) introduces additional compute overhead during the training loop.

Crucial hyper-parameters such as the choice of sliding window size $L$, scaling factor $\lambda_{seg}$, and optimization steps for the 'fake' score estimator are not thoroughly analyzed via sensitivity curves in the ablation studies.

strengths: Well-motivated paradigm that decouples local realism (mode-seeking) from global coherence (mean-seeking) to solve the fidelity-horizon trade-off in long video generation.
The decoupled dual-head architecture (FM and DM heads sharing a long-context encoder) effectively resolves the gradient interference between the SFT and distillation objectives.
Achieves high-quality, long-form video generation (up to 60 seconds) with exceptional efficiency, operating as a few-step generator (NFE=4).
Comprehensive and thorough evaluation including standard VBench-Long metrics, MLLM (Gemini) consistency evaluations, 60-second stress tests, and a user study with 31 participants.
weaknesses: Training complexity is high; on-policy rollouts for sliding window DMD combined with SFT and sequence parallelism suggest a heavy training cost, which lacks a detailed compute and training time breakdown.

The use of an online estimator ($v_{fake}$) trained for 5 steps between student updates can be highly unstable in practice. The paper does not provide detailed analysis of training stability, sensitivity, or hyperparameter choices for this step.
Architectural novelty is slightly limited as it heavily borrows from the Decoupled Diffusion Transformer (DDT) framework, though the application to long-video sliding-window distillation is novel.
